exampleAnswers.title: Calculating the Determinant of a Product

question.explanation:
Given two $n\times n$ matrices $M$ and $N,$ we have

\[ \det(M N) = \det(M) \cdot \det(N). \]

In our case, this gives \begin{align*} \det(A) &= \det \begin{bmatrix} 4 & -6 & 5 \\ 0 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 5 \end{bmatrix} \cdot \det \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ -5 & -2 & 0\\ 6 & 2 & 1 \end{bmatrix}. \end{align*}

Notice that both matrices are triangular. Therefore, we obtain

\begin{align*} \det(A) &= \big(4 \cdot (-2) \cdot 5\big) \cdot \big( 1 \cdot (-2) \cdot 1 \big) \\[3pt] &=(-40) \cdot (-2) \\[3pt] &= 80. \end{align*}

question.explanation:
Given two $n\times n$ matrices $M$ and $N,$ we have

\[ \det(M N) = \det(M) \cdot \det(N). \]

In our case, this gives \[ \det(C) = \det \begin{bmatrix} 6 & 2 & -2 \\ 2 & 1 & 4 \\ 0 & 0 & 2 \end{bmatrix} \cdot \det \begin{bmatrix} 4 & 0 & 5 \\ -6 & -1 & 2\\ 1 & 0 & 3 \end{bmatrix}. \]

We can compute the required determinants as follows:

  • For the first determinant, we can compute it using a Laplace expansion across the $3$rd row.

  • For the second determinant, we can compute it using a Laplace expansion down the $2$nd column.

Therefore, we obtain

\begin{align*} \det(C) &= \begin{vmatrix} 6 & 2 & -2 \\ 2 & 1 & 4 \\ \color{blue}0 & \color{blue}0 & {\color{blue}2} \end{vmatrix} \cdot \begin{vmatrix} 4 & \color{blue}0 & 5 \\ -6 & {\color{blue}-1} & 2\\ 1 & \color{blue}0 & 3 \end{vmatrix} \\[5pt] &= 2(-1)^{3+3} \begin{vmatrix} 6 & 2 \\ 2 & 1 \end{vmatrix} \cdot (-1)(-1)^{2+2} \begin{vmatrix} 4 & 5 \\ 1 & 3 \end{vmatrix}\\[5pt] &=2(6-4)\cdot(-1)(12-5) \\[5pt] &=4\cdot (-7)\\[5pt] &= -28. \end{align*}

question.explanation:
Given two $n\times n$ matrices $M$ and $N,$ we have

\[ \det(M N) = \det(M) \cdot \det(N). \]

In our case, this gives

\[ \det(A) = \det \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 2 \\ 1 & -1 & 2 \\ 1 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \cdot \det \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 & 1 \\ -2 & 1 & 3\\ 0 & 0 & 2 \end{bmatrix}. \]

We can compute the required determinants as follows:

  • For the first determinant, we can compute it using a Laplace expansion down the $2$nd column.

  • For the second determinant, we can compute it using a Laplace expansion across the $3$rd row.

Therefore, we obtain

\begin{align*} \det(A) &= \begin{vmatrix} 1 & \color{blue}0 & 2 \\ 1 &\color{blue} -1 & 2 \\ 1 & \color{blue}0 & 1 \end{vmatrix} \cdot \begin{vmatrix} 1 & 1 & 1 \\ -2 & 1 & 3\\ \color{blue}0 & \color{blue}0 & \color{blue}2 \end{vmatrix} \\[5pt] &= (-1)(-1)^{2+2} \begin{vmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 1 & 1 \end{vmatrix} \cdot 2(-1)^{3+3} \begin{vmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ -2 & 1 \end{vmatrix}\\[5pt] &=-(1-2) \cdot 2(1+2) \\[5pt] &= 1\cdot 6\\[5pt] &=6. \end{align*}

exampleAnswers.title: Calculating the Determinant of the Inverse of a Matrix

question.text: Let $A,$ $B,$ and $C$ be square matrices. If $A = B\cdot C,$ $|B|=9$ and $|C^{-1}|=-3$, find $|A|.$
question.explanation:
Given two $n\times n$ matrices $M$ and $N,$ we have

\[ \det(MN) = \det(M)\cdot \det(N). \]

Also, given an invertible $n\times n$ matrix $M,$ we have

\[ \det\left(M^{-1}\right) = \dfrac{1}{\det(M)}. \]

Since $|C|=\dfrac{1}{|C^{-1}|}$, we get $|C| = -\dfrac{1}{3}.$

Therefore, we obtain

\begin{align} |A| & = |B|\cdot |C| \\[5pt] & = 9 \cdot \left(-\dfrac 1 3\right) \\[5pt] & = -3. \end{align}

example.title: Calculating the Determinant of the Inverse of a Matrix

question.explanation:
Given an invertible $n\times n$ matrix $A,$ we have

\[ \det\left(A^{-1}\right) = \dfrac{1}{\det(A)}. \]

First, we find $\det(A)\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} \det(A) &= \det \begin{bmatrix} 4 & 3 \\ 6 & 5 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &=20-18 \\[5pt] &= 2 \end{align*} Therefore, we obtain

\[ \det(A^{-1}) = \dfrac{1}{\det(A)} =\dfrac{1}{2}.\]

example.title: Calculating the Determinant of the Inverse of a Matrix

question.explanation:
Given an invertible $n\times n$ matrix $A,$ we have

\[ \det\left(A^{-1}\right) = \dfrac{1}{\det(A)}. \]

First, we find $\det(A)\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} \det(A) &= \det \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 5 & 5 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &=10 -5 \\[5pt] &= 5 \end{align*}

Therefore, we obtain

\[ \det(A^{-1}) = \dfrac{1}{\det(A)} = \dfrac{1}{5}. \]

example.title: Calculating the Determinant of the Inverse of a Matrix

question.explanation:
Given an invertible $n\times n$ matrix $A,$ we have

\[ |A^{-1}| = \dfrac{1}{|A|}. \]

First, we find $|A|$ using a Laplace expansion across the $3$rd row:

\begin{align*} |A| &= \begin{vmatrix} -7& 3 & 5 \\ 6 & -4 & 1\\ -2 & 0 & 0 \end{vmatrix} \\[5pt] &=-2 \cdot (-1)^{3+1} \cdot \begin{vmatrix} 3& 5 \\ -4 & 1 \end{vmatrix} \\[5pt] &=(-2) \cdot (3+20) \\[5pt] &=-46 \end{align*}

Therefore, we obtain

\[ |A^{-1}|=\dfrac{1}{|A|}=-\dfrac{1}{46}.\]

example.title: Calculating the Determinant of the Inverse of a Matrix

question.explanation:
Given an invertible $n\times n$ matrix $A,$ we have

\[ |A^{-1}| = \dfrac{1}{|A|}. \]

First, we find $|A|$ using a Laplace expansion across the $2$nd column:

\begin{align*} |A| &= \begin{vmatrix} 3 & 2 & 5 \\ -4 & 1 & -2\\ 1 & -1 & 3 \end{vmatrix} \\[5pt] &=2(-1)^{1+2} \begin{vmatrix} -4 & -2\\ 1 & 3 \end{vmatrix}+ 1(-1)^{2+2} \begin{vmatrix} 3 & 5 \\ 1 & 3 \end{vmatrix} +(-1)(-1)^{3+2} \begin{vmatrix} 3 & 5 \\ -4 & -2 \end{vmatrix} \\[5pt] &= -2(-12+2)+(9-5)+(-6+20) \\[5pt] &= 20 + 4 + 14 \\[5pt] &= 38 \end{align*}

Therefore, we obtain

\[ |A^{-1}|=\dfrac{1}{|A|}=\dfrac{1}{38}. \]

exampleAnswers.title: Calculating a Determinant Using the Linearity of the Determinant

question.text: Given that $ \begin{vmatrix} a& b & c \\ 3 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 \end{vmatrix} = 4, $ find $ \begin{vmatrix} a+1 & b & c \\ 3 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 \end{vmatrix}. $
question.explanation:
We "factor out" the given determinant from the determinant we would like to find:

\begin{align*} \begin{vmatrix} a+1 & b & c \\ 3 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 \end{vmatrix} &= \begin{vmatrix} {\color{red}a}+{\color{blue}1} & {\color{red}b}+{\color{blue}0} & {\color{red}c}+{\color{blue}0} \\ 3 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 \end{vmatrix} \\[2pt] \end{align*}

Now, using the linearity property of determinants and expanding the second determinant across the $1$st row, we obtain

\begin{align*} \begin{vmatrix} {\color{red}a}+{\color{blue}1} & {\color{red}b}+{\color{blue}0} & {\color{red}c}+{\color{blue}0} \\ 3 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 \end{vmatrix} &= \underbrace{ \begin{vmatrix} {\color{red}a} & {\color{red}b} & {\color{red}c} \\ 3 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 \end{vmatrix} }_{\large 4} + \begin{vmatrix} {\color{blue}1} & {\color{blue}0} & {\color{blue}0} \\ 3 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 \end{vmatrix} \\[5pt] &= 4 + 1(-1)^{1+1} \begin{vmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 \end{vmatrix} \\[5pt] &= 4+1 \\[5pt] &= 5. \end{align*}

example.title: Calculating a Determinant Using the Linearity of the Determinant

question.explanation:
First, notice that the $1$st row of our determinant is almost equal to the $2$nd row. So, we can rewrite the given determinant, as follows:

\begin{align*} \begin{vmatrix} 300 & 250 & 100 \\ 300 & 270 & 100 \\ 1 &-1 & 1 \end{vmatrix} &= \begin{vmatrix} {\color{red}300} & {\color{red}250} & {\color{red}100} \\ {\color{red}300}+{\color{blue}0} & {\color{red}250}+{\color{blue}20} & {\color{red}100}+{\color{blue}0} \\ 1 &-1 & 1 \end{vmatrix} \end{align*}

Next, using the linearity property of determinants, we obtain

\begin{align*} \begin{vmatrix} {\color{red}300} & {\color{red}250} & {\color{red}100} \\ {\color{red}300}+{\color{blue}0} & {\color{red}250}+{\color{blue}20} & {\color{red}100}+{\color{blue}0} \\ 1 &-1 & 1 \end{vmatrix} &= \begin{vmatrix} {\color{red}300} & {\color{red}250} & {\color{red}100} \\ {\color{red}300} & {\color{red}250} & {\color{red}100} \\ 1 &-1 & 1 \end{vmatrix} + \begin{vmatrix} {\color{red}300} & {\color{red}250} & {\color{red}100} \\ {\color{blue}0} &{\color{blue}20} &{\color{blue}0} \\ 1 &-1 & 1 \end{vmatrix}. \end{align*}

The first determinant must be zero since it has two identical rows, while the second determinant can be expanded across the $2$nd row, as follows:

\begin{align*} \begin{vmatrix} {\color{red}300} & {\color{red}250} & {\color{red}100} \\ {\color{red}300} & {\color{red}250} & {\color{red}100} \\ 1 &-1 & 1 \end{vmatrix} + \begin{vmatrix} {\color{red}300} & {\color{red}250} & {\color{red}100} \\ {\color{blue}0} &{\color{blue}20} &{\color{blue}0} \\ 1 &-1 & 1 \end{vmatrix} &= 0 +20(-1)^{2+2} \begin{vmatrix} 300 & 100 \\ 1 & 1 \end{vmatrix}\\[5pt] & = 20\cdot(300 \cdot 1 - 100 \cdot 1) \\[5pt] &= 20\cdot 200\\[5pt] &= 4\, 000 \end{align*}

question.text: Given that $ \begin{vmatrix} a+2 & -2&2 \\ b+3 & 4 &2\\ c & 0& 1 \end{vmatrix} = 5, $ find $ \begin{vmatrix} a+1 & -2&2 \\ b & 4 &2\\ c & 0& 1 \end{vmatrix}. $
question.explanation:
We "factor out" the given determinant from the determinant we would like to find: \begin{align*} \begin{vmatrix} a+1 & -2&2 \\ b & 4 &2\\ c & 0& 1 \end{vmatrix} &= \begin{vmatrix} {\color{red}(a+2)}-{\color{blue}1} & -2&2 \\ {\color{red}(b+3)}-{\color{blue}3}& 4 &2\\ {\color{red}c}+{\color{blue}0}& 0& 1 \end{vmatrix} \end{align*}

Now, using the linearity property of determinants and expanding the second determinant across the $3$rd row, we obtain

\begin{align*} \begin{vmatrix} {\color{red}(a+2)}-{\color{blue}1} & -2&2 \\ {\color{red}(b+3)}-{\color{blue}3}& 4 &2\\ {\color{red}c}+{\color{blue}0}& 0& 1 \end{vmatrix} &=\underbrace{ \begin{vmatrix} {\color{red}(a+2)} & -2&2 \\ {\color{red}(b+3)}& 4 &2\\ {\color{red}c} & 0& 1 \end{vmatrix} }_{\large 5} + \begin{vmatrix} -{1} & -2&2 \\ -{3} & 4 &2\\ {\color{blue}0} & \color{blue}0 & \color{blue}1 \end{vmatrix} \\[5pt] &= 5+1\cdot(-1)^{3+3}\begin{vmatrix} -1& -2 \\ -3 & 4 \end{vmatrix} \\[5pt] &= 5+(-10)\\[5pt] &=-5. \end{align*}

example.title: Calculating a Determinant Using the Linearity of the Determinant

question.explanation:
First, notice that the $2$nd row of our determinant is almost equal to the $3$rd row. So, we can rewrite the given determinant, as follows:

\begin{align*} \begin{vmatrix} 8 & 4 & 2 \\ 114 & 210 & 198 \\ 113& 210 & 198 \end{vmatrix} &= \begin{vmatrix} 8 & 4 & 2 \\ {\color{red}113}+{\color{blue}1} & {\color{red}210}+{\color{blue}0} & {\color{red}198}+{\color{blue}0} \\ {\color{red}113} & {\color{red}210} & {\color{red}198} \end{vmatrix} \end{align*}

Next, using the linearity property of determinants, we obtain

\begin{align*} \begin{vmatrix} 8 & 4 & 2 \\ {\color{red}113}+{\color{blue}1} & {\color{red}210}+{\color{blue}0} & {\color{red}198}+{\color{blue}0} \\ {\color{red}113} & {\color{red}210} & {\color{red}198} \end{vmatrix} &= \begin{vmatrix} 8 & 4 & 2 \\ {\color{red}113} & {\color{red}210} & {\color{red}198} \\ {\color{red}113} & {\color{red}210} & {\color{red}198} \end{vmatrix} + \begin{vmatrix} 8 & 4 & 2 \\ {\color{blue}1} & {\color{blue}0} &{\color{blue}0} \\ {\color{red}113} & {\color{red}210} & {\color{red}198} \end{vmatrix} . \end{align*}

The first determinant must be zero since it has two identical rows, while the second determinant can be expanded across the $2$nd row, as follows:

\begin{align*} \begin{vmatrix} 8 & 4 & 2 \\ {\color{red}113} & {\color{red}210} & {\color{red}198} \\ {\color{red}113} & {\color{red}210} & {\color{red}198} \end{vmatrix} + \begin{vmatrix} 8 & 4 & 2 \\ {\color{blue}1} & {\color{blue}0} &{\color{blue}0} \\ {\color{red}113} & {\color{red}210} & {\color{red}198} \end{vmatrix} &= 0 +1(-1)^{2+1} \begin{vmatrix} 4& 2 \\ 210 & 198 \end{vmatrix}\\[5pt] & = -(4\cdot 198-2\cdot 210) \\[2pt] &= -(792-420)\\[5pt] &= -372 \end{align*}

example.title: Calculating a Determinant Using the Linearity of the Determinant

question.explanation:
First, notice that the $1$st row of our determinant is almost equal to the $3$rd row. So, we can rewrite the given determinant, as follows:

\begin{align*} \begin{vmatrix} 107 & 215 & 99 \\ 6 & 8 & 11 \\ 107 & 215 & 100 \end{vmatrix} &= \begin{vmatrix} {\color{red}107} & {\color{red}215} & {\color{red}99} \\ 6 & 8 & 11 \\ {\color{red}107}+{\color{blue}0} & {\color{red}215}+{\color{blue}0} & {\color{red}99}+{\color{blue}1} \end{vmatrix} \end{align*}

Next, using the linearity property of determinants, we obtain

\begin{align*} \begin{vmatrix} {\color{red}107} & {\color{red}215} & {\color{red}99} \\ 6 & 8 & 11 \\ {\color{red}107}+{\color{blue}0} & {\color{red}215}+{\color{blue}0} & {\color{red}99}+{\color{blue}1} \end{vmatrix} &= \begin{vmatrix} {\color{red}107} & {\color{red}215} & {\color{red}99} \\ 6 & 8 & 11 \\ {\color{red}107} & {\color{red}215} & {\color{red}99} \\ \end{vmatrix} + \begin{vmatrix} 107 & 215 & 99 \\ 6 & 8 & 11 \\ {\color{blue}0} & {\color{blue}0} & {\color{blue}1} \end{vmatrix}. \end{align*}

The first determinant must be zero since it has two identical rows, while the second determinant can be expanded across the $3$rd row, as follows:

\begin{align*} \begin{vmatrix} {\color{red}107} & {\color{red}215} & {\color{red}99} \\ 6 & 8 & 11 \\ {\color{red}107} & {\color{red}215} & {\color{red}99} \\ \end{vmatrix} + \begin{vmatrix} 107 & 215 & 99 \\ 6 & 8 & 11 \\ {\color{blue}0} & {\color{blue}0} & {\color{blue}1} \end{vmatrix} &= 0 +1(-1)^{3+3} \begin{vmatrix} 107 & 215 \\ 6 & 8 \end{vmatrix}\\[5pt] & = 107 \cdot 8 - 215 \cdot 6 \\[5pt] &= -434 \end{align*}
